seo.shortDescription: Searchable 2026 U.S. tariff table for all 319 HTS Chapter 39 lines — polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC and PET resin, plastic film, vinyl flooring, plastic bags and packaging, tableware and other plastic articles. Base rates Free to 6.5% plus the extra duty by country: 10%–12.5% under Section 301, up to 44% from China, 50% Section 338 on some Canadian goods.

overview.intro:
Chapter 39 covers plastics in two forms. **Primary forms** (headings 3901–3914) are the resins themselves — polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, polystyrene, PET, epoxy and other polymers in pellets, powders and liquids. **Articles** (3915–3926) are what is made from them: scrap, pipes and hoses, vinyl flooring, tape, film and sheet, foam, packaging, bags and bottles, tableware, builders' ware and every other article of plastics. Base rates are low: **33 of the 319 lines are Free and none is above 6.5%**.

The U.S. imported **$74.02B** of these goods in 2025: $17.71B of resins and the rest articles. **China** ($16.87B) and **Canada** ($12.77B) supplied 40%, ahead of Mexico, Vietnam and South Korea. On top of the base rate comes the **extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies — +10% for Canada, Mexico, India and the UK (USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt), +12.5% for Vietnam and Thailand, **12.5% in total** for Korea and Japan and **10% in total** for the EU and Taiwan. **China pays +12.5% plus its 2018–2019 Section 301 lists** — +25% on most resins, film and packaging, +7.5% on some household goods — so most Chinese plastics pay 37.5% to 44%. Twenty Canadian subheadings, among them plastic bags, bottles, closures, tableware and vinyl tile, owe a **50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA**. On top of all this, **antidumping and countervailing duty orders** cover PET resin, PET film, polyethylene carrier bags, epoxy resins, PVA, PTFE, polypropylene corrugated boxes, fiberglass door panels and other goods from named countries.

productGroups.label: Polyethylene & other ethylene polymers, in primary forms
productGroups.blurb: Low-density, linear low-density and high-density polyethylene (LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE), EVA and other ethylene copolymers in pellets or powder. Mostly 6.5%. Canada supplied $2.97B of the $3.77B imported in 2025 — Free under USMCA and not on the Section 338 list. China List 2 (+25%) except 3901.40 (List 3).

productGroups.label: Polypropylene & other olefin polymers, in primary forms
productGroups.blurb: Polypropylene, polyisobutylene and propylene copolymers. 6.5%; elastomeric polyisobutylene (3902.20.10) Free. China List 2.

productGroups.label: Polystyrene, SAN & ABS, in primary forms
productGroups.blurb: Polystyrene (expandable or not), styrene-acrylonitrile (SAN) and acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS). All 6.5%. China List 2.

productGroups.label: PVC, PTFE & other halogenated polymers, in primary forms
productGroups.blurb: PVC resin (6.5%), mixed and plasticized PVC compounds, vinylidene chloride polymers and fluoropolymers such as PTFE (5.8%) and PFA. Granular PTFE from India and Russia carries antidumping and countervailing duties; PFA from India is under investigation. PVC is a CBP forced-labor high-priority sector.

productGroups.label: Polyvinyl acetate, polyvinyl alcohol & other vinyl polymers
productGroups.blurb: Polyvinyl acetate dispersions, vinyl acetate copolymers and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, 3.2%). Free to 5.3%. PVA from China and Japan carries antidumping duties (orders continued September 18, 2026).

productGroups.label: Acrylic polymers, in primary forms
productGroups.blurb: Acrylic polymers: poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) pellets, acrylic dispersions and superabsorbent polymers. Free to 6.3%. China List 2.

productGroups.label: PET, polycarbonates, epoxy resins, polyethers & other polyesters
productGroups.blurb: PET bottle resin (3907.61, 6.5%), polycarbonates, epoxy resins (6.1%), polyacetals, polyethers, PLA, alkyds and other polyesters. Korea is the top supplier ($851M in 2025). Antidumping duties apply to PET resin from Canada, China, India and Oman and to epoxy resins from Korea, Taiwan and Thailand; acrylate oligomers and PTMEG are covered or under investigation too.

productGroups.label: Polyamides (nylon), in primary forms
productGroups.blurb: Polyamides in primary forms: nylon 6, 6/6, 11 and 12 pellets (3908.10, 6.3%); other polyamides Free or 6.5%. China List 2.

productGroups.label: Amino resins, phenolic resins & polyurethanes
productGroups.blurb: Urea, melamine and phenolic resins and polyurethanes, including MDI-based polymers. Mostly 6.5%. China List 2, List 3 for 3909.31 and 3909.39.

productGroups.label: Silicones, in primary forms
productGroups.blurb: Silicones in primary forms — silicone oils, rubbers and resins. 3%. China List 2.

productGroups.label: Petroleum resins, polyterpenes & other resins
productGroups.blurb: Petroleum hydrocarbon resins, coumarone-indene, polyterpenes, polysulfides, polysulfones and other resins. Free to 6.5%. China List 2.

productGroups.label: Cellulose & its chemical derivatives
productGroups.blurb: Cellulose acetates, cellulose nitrate, carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) and other cellulose ethers. 4.2%–6.4%. China List 2 or List 3.

productGroups.label: Natural polymers (alginates) & modified natural polymers
productGroups.blurb: Alginic acid and sodium alginate (4.2%), and modified natural polymers such as hardened proteins. China List 4A for alginates (an exclusion covers sodium alginate resins through November 9, 2026), List 2 or 3 for the rest.

productGroups.label: Ion-exchange resins
productGroups.blurb: Ion-exchange resins based on polymers of 3901–3913. Free or 3.9%. China List 2.

productGroups.label: Plastic waste, parings & scrap
productGroups.blurb: Waste, parings and scrap of polyethylene, polystyrene, PVC and other plastics. All Free; China List 3 adds 25%.

productGroups.label: Monofilament, rods, sticks & profile shapes
productGroups.blurb: Monofilament over 1 mm, rods, sticks and profile shapes, such as PVC profiles and plastic edge banding. 3.1%–6.5%. Canada supplied $499M in 2025.

productGroups.label: Tubes, pipes, hoses & their fittings
productGroups.blurb: Rigid and flexible tubes, pipes and hoses — PVC, polyethylene and polypropylene pipe, garden hose, sausage casings — and their fittings. 3.1% for most pipe and hose, 5.3% for fittings. Civil-aircraft hoses and tubes qualify for the aircraft exemptions.

productGroups.label: Floor, wall & ceiling coverings, incl. vinyl flooring
productGroups.blurb: Floor, wall and ceiling coverings in rolls or tiles: luxury vinyl tile and plank (LVT/SPC, 3918.10.10, 5.3%), vinyl sheet flooring and vinyl wall coverings. Vietnam supplied $2.19B of the $4.79B imported in 2025. China List 3; 3918.10.10 from Canada is on the Section 338 list.

productGroups.label: Self-adhesive tape, film, labels & other flat shapes
productGroups.blurb: Self-adhesive plates, sheets, film, tape and strip: packing tape, electrical tape, labels and protective film. 5.8%, 6.5% for reflective tape. China List 2 (some polyethylene adhesive films are excluded through November 9, 2026).

productGroups.label: Film, sheet & strip, non-cellular and not reinforced
productGroups.blurb: Non-cellular film, sheet and strip: polyethylene film (4.2%), polypropylene film (4.2%), PVC film, acrylic sheet, polycarbonate sheet and PET film (4.2%). PET film from China, India, Taiwan and the UAE carries antidumping duties. China List 2.

productGroups.label: Foam & other plastic sheet, film & strip
productGroups.blurb: Cellular (foam) sheet of polystyrene, PVC and polyurethane, and other film or sheet combined with other materials. 4.2%–6.5%. China List 2.

productGroups.label: Baths, sinks, toilet seats & other sanitary ware
productGroups.blurb: Baths, shower bases, sinks, washbasins, toilet seats and covers and other sanitary ware of plastics. All 6.3%. China List 4A (+7.5%) on baths, sinks and toilet seats, List 3 on the rest.

productGroups.label: Packaging: boxes, bags, bottles, caps & closures
productGroups.blurb: Plastic packaging: boxes and crates, polyethylene bags and sacks (3923.21), bottles (3923.30), caps and closures (3923.50) and other containers. 3% for most, 5.3% for closures and spools. Polyethylene retail carrier bags (3923.21.00.85) carry antidumping duties from six countries. Canada, China and Mexico each supplied over $1.7B in 2025.

productGroups.label: Tableware, kitchenware & household articles
productGroups.blurb: Tableware and kitchenware (plates and cups 6.5%, trays 5.3%, other 3.4%) and other household and toilet articles such as storage containers, hangers and shower curtains. China supplied $5.71B of the $7.65B imported in 2025; most lines pay +7.5% (List 4A) or nothing under the old China lists.

productGroups.label: Builders' ware: tanks, doors, windows, shutters
productGroups.blurb: Builders' ware: tanks over 300 liters (6.3%), doors, windows and frames (5.3%), shutters and blinds, and other building fittings. Fiberglass door panels from China carry antidumping and countervailing duties since August 6, 2026.

productGroups.label: Other articles: office supplies, gloves, fittings, gaskets
productGroups.blurb: Every other article of plastics: office and school supplies, apparel and gloves (seamless gloves Free), furniture fittings, statuettes, gaskets and seals, laboratory ware, face shields and the catch-all 3926.90.99 (5.3%). The largest heading — $14.61B in 2025, $5.84B of it from China.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: Polyethylene film from China
workedExamples.body: Film and sheet of polymers of ethylene pay 4.2%. China adds +12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31) and +25% because 3920.10 is on List 2 (9903.88.02): **41.7%**, $4,170 on a $10,000 shipment. The same film pays 14.2% from India or the UK, 16.7% from Vietnam or Thailand, 10% in total from Germany or Taiwan, 12.5% from Korea or Japan, and nothing from Canada or Mexico under USMCA.

workedExamples.title: Polyethylene retail carrier bags from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Sacks and bags of polymers of ethylene pay 3%; Vietnam adds +12.5% (9903.05.84): **15.5%**, $1,550 on $10,000. Retail carrier bags with handles from Vietnam are also covered by an antidumping order and a countervailing duty order (continued October 27, 2021, 86 FR 59366), so CBP collects a cash deposit at the rate Commerce set for the exporter on top. From China the bag pays 40.5% (3% + 12.5% + 25% List 3) plus the China antidumping duty.

workedExamples.title: Vinyl plank flooring (rigid core) from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Vinyl tile pays 5.3%. Vietnam adds +12.5%: **17.8%**, $1,780 on $10,000. From China it pays 42.8% (List 3 +25%), from Korea 12.5% in total, from Thailand 17.8%. From Canada vinyl tile is on the Section 338 list: 50% even with a USMCA claim. PVC is a forced-labor high-priority sector, so CBP can ask for supply-chain records back to the PVC resin.

workedExamples.title: Plastic food storage containers from China
workedExamples.body: Other plastic tableware and kitchenware pays 3.4%. This line is on none of the 2018–2019 China lists, so China pays only the 2026 Section 301 duty: 3.4% + 12.5% = **15.9%**. Plastic plates and cups (3924.10.20, 6.5%) are on List 4A: 6.5% + 12.5% + 7.5% = 26.5%. Food-contact plastics must be made of substances FDA permits (21 CFR parts 174–178).

workedExamples.title: HDPE resin and plastic bags from Canada
workedExamples.body: HDPE pays 6.5%. A USMCA-qualifying shipment from Canada pays **nothing** — 3901.20 is not on the Section 338 list — while a non-qualifying one pays 6.5% + 10% = 16.5%. Polyethylene bags (3923.21) from Canada are on the Section 338 list: 50% even under USMCA (U.S. note 51(a)), 63% without it.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** Throughout the tariff schedule the expression "plastics" means those materials of headings 3901 to 3914 which are or have been capable, either at the moment of polymerization or at some subsequent stage, of being formed under external influence (usually heat and pressure, if necessary with a solvent or plasticizer) by molding, casting, extruding, rolling or other process into shapes which are retained on the removal of the external influence. Throughout the tariff schedule, any reference to "plastics" also includes vulcanized fiber. The expression, however, does not apply to materials regarded as textile materials of section XI.

**Note 2.** This chapter does not cover: (a) Lubricating preparations of 2710 or 3403; (b) Waxes of heading 2712 or 3404; (c) Separate chemically defined organic compounds (chapter 29); (d) Heparin or its salts (heading 3001); (e) Solutions (other than collodions) consisting of any of the products specified in headings 3901 to 3913 in volatile organic solvents when the weight of the solvent exceeds 50 percent of the weight of the solution (heading 3208); stamping foils of heading 3212; (f) Organic surface-active agents or preparations of heading 3402; (g) Run gums or ester gums (heading 3806); (h) Prepared additives for mineral oils (including gasoline) or for other liquids used for the same purposes as mineral oil (heading 3811); (ij) Prepared hydraulic fluids based on polyglycols, silicones or other polymers of Chapter 39 (heading 3819); (k) Diagnostic or laboratory reagents on a backing of plastics (heading 3822); (l) Synthetic rubber, as defined for the purposes of chapter 40, or articles thereof; (m) Saddlery or harness (heading 4201) or trunks, suitcases, handbags or other containers of heading 4202; (n) Plaits, wickerwork or other articles of chapter 46; (o) Wall coverings of heading 4814; (p) Goods of section XI (textiles and textile articles); (q) Articles of section XII (for example, footwear, headgear, umbrellas, sun umbrellas, walking-sticks, whips, riding-crops or parts thereof); (r) Imitation jewelry of heading 7117; (s) Articles of section XVI (machines and mechanical or electrical appliances); (t) Parts of aircraft or vehicles of section XVII; (u) Articles of chapter 90 (for example, optical elements, spectacle frames, drawing instruments); (v) Articles of chapter 91 (for example, clock or watch cases); (w) Articles of chapter 92 (for example, musical instruments or parts thereof); (x) Articles of chapter 94 (for example, furniture, luminaires and lighting fittings, illuminated signs, prefabricated buildings); (y) Articles of chapter 95 (for example, toys, games, sports equipment); or (z) Articles of chapter 96 (for example, brushes, buttons, slide fasteners, combs, mouthpieces or stems for smoking pipes, cigarette holders or the like, parts of vacuum flasks or the like, pens, mechanical pencils, and monopods, bipods, tripods and similar articles).

**Note 3.** Headings 3901 to 3911 apply only to goods of a kind produced by chemical synthesis, falling in the following categories: (a) Liquid synthetic polyolefins of which less than 60 percent by volume distills at 300°C, after conversion to 1,013 millibars when a reduced-pressure distillation method is used (headings 3901 and 3902); (b) Resins, not highly polymerized, of the coumarone-indene type (heading 3911); (c) Other synthetic polymers with an average of at least five monomer units; (d) Silicones (heading 3910); (e) Resols (heading 3909) and other prepolymers.

**Note 4.** The expression "copolymers" covers all polymers in which no single monomer contributes 95 percent or more by weight to the total polymer content. For the purposes of this chapter, except where the context otherwise requires, copolymers (including co-polycondensates, co-polyaddition products, block copolymers and graft copolymers) and polymer blends are to be classified in the heading covering polymers of that comonomer unit which predominates by weight over every other single comonomer unit. For the purposes of this note, constituent comonomer units of polymers falling in the same heading shall be taken together. If no single comonomer predominates, copolymers or polymer blends, as the case may be, are to be classified in the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration.

**Note 5.** Chemically modified polymers, that is, those in which only appendages to the main polymer chain have been changed by chemical reaction, are to be classified in the heading appropriate to the unmodified polymer. This provision does not apply to graft copolymers.

**Note 6.** In headings 3901 to 3914, the expression "primary forms" applies only to the following forms: (a) Liquids and pastes, including dispersions (emulsions and suspensions) and solutions; (b) Blocks of irregular shape, lumps, powders (including molding powders), granules, flakes and similar bulk forms.

**Note 7.** Heading 3915 does not apply to waste, parings and scrap of a single thermoplastic material, transformed into primary forms (headings 3901 to 3914).

**Note 8.** For the purposes of heading 3917, the expression "tubes, pipes and hoses" means hollow products, whether semimanufactures or finished products, of a kind generally used for conveying, conducting or distributing gases or liquids (for example, ribbed garden hose, perforated tubes). This expression also includes sausage casings and other lay-flat tubing. However, except for the last mentioned, those having an internal cross section other than round, oval, rectangular (in which the length does not exceed 1.5 times the width) or in the shape of a regular polygon are not to be regarded as tubes, pipes and hoses, but as profile shapes.

**Note 9.** For the purposes of heading 3918, the expression "wall or ceiling coverings of plastics" applies to products in rolls, of a width not less than 45 cm, suitable for wall or ceiling decoration, consisting of plastics fixed permanently on a backing of any material other than paper, the layer of plastics (on the face side) being grained, embossed, colored, design-printed or otherwise decorated.

**Note 10.** In headings 3920 and 3921, the expression "plates, sheets, film, foil and strip" applies only to plates, sheets, film, foil and strip (other than those of chapter 54) and to blocks of regular geometric shape, whether or not printed or otherwise surface-worked, uncut or cut into rectangles (including squares) but not further worked (even if when so cut they become articles ready for use).

**Note 11.** Heading 3925 applies only to the following articles, not being products covered by any of the earlier headings of subchapter II: (a) Reservoirs, tanks (including septic tanks), vats and similar containers, of a capacity exceeding 300 liters; (b) Structural elements used, for example, in floors, walls or partitions, ceilings or roofs; (c) Gutters and fittings therefor; (d) Doors, windows and their frames and thresholds for doors; (e) Balconies, balustrades, fencing, gates and similar barriers; (f) Shutters, blinds (including venetian blinds) and similar articles and parts and fittings thereof; (g) Large-scale shelving for assembly and permanent installation, for example, in shops, workshops, warehouses; (h) Ornamental architectural features, for example, flutings, cupolas, dovecotes; and (ij) Fittings and mountings intended for permanent installation in or on doors, windows, staircases, walls or other parts of buildings, for example, knobs, handles, hooks, brackets, towel rails, switch plates and other protective plates.

**Subheading note 1.** Within any one heading of this chapter, polymers (including copolymers) are to be classified according to the following provisions: (a) Where there is a subheading named "Other" in the same series: (1) The designation in a subheading of a polymer by the prefix "poly" (for example, polyethylene and polyamide-6,6) means that the constituent monomer unit or monomer units of the named polymer taken together must contribute 95 percent or more by weight of the total polymer content. (2) The copolymers named in subheadings 3901.30, 3901.40, 3903.20, 3903.30 and 3904.30 are to be classified in those subheadings, provided that the comonomer units of the named copolymers contribute 95 percent or more by weight of the total polymer content. (3) Chemically modified polymers are to be classified in the subheading named "Other", provided that the chemically modified polymers are not more specifically covered by another subheading. (4) Polymers not meeting (1), (2), or (3), above, are to be classified in the subheading, among the remaining subheadings in the series, covering polymers of that monomer unit which predominates by weight over every other single comonomer unit. For this purpose, constituent monomer units of polymers falling in the same subheading shall be taken together. Only the constituent comonomer units of the polymers in the series of subheadings under consideration are to be compared. (b) Where there is no subheading named "Other" in the same series: (1) Polymers are to be classified in the subheading covering polymers of that monomer unit which predominates by weight over every other single comonomer unit. For this purpose, constituent monomer units of polymers falling in the same subheading shall be taken together. Only the constituent comonomer units of the polymers in the series under consideration are to be compared. (2) Chemically modified polymers are to be classified in the subheading appropriate to the unmodified polymer. Polymer blends are to be classified in the same subheading as polymers of the same monomer units in the same proportions.

**Subheading note 2.** For the purposes of subheading 3920.43, the term “plasticizers” includes secondary plasticizers.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 39: Plastics & Articles of Plastics — Tariff Updates 2025–2026

seo.title: Plastics Tariff Updates 2026 (HTS Chapter 39): Section 301 by Country, China Lists, Canada Section 338, AD/CVD on PET Resin & Bags | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every 2025–2026 change to U.S. tariffs on plastic resins, film, bags, flooring and other Chapter 39 goods, with dates and official sources: the end of the IEEPA duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, China List 2/3/4A, the Canada Section 338 duty, and antidumping orders on PET resin, PET film, carrier bags, epoxy and more.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 39 base rate changed**: all 317 lines in both editions carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates, from Free to 6.5%. The only change is statistical: from July 1, 2026 laboratory ware of 3926.90.99 is split into separatory funnels (3926.90.99.15) and other laboratory ware (3926.90.99.20).

Everything that changed sits on top of the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA duties reached plastics from almost every country — up to 145% for China in April–May 2025 on top of its Section 301 lists, 25%–35% on non-USMCA goods from Mexico and Canada, 19%–20% for most of Southeast Asia, 15% in total for the EU and Japan — though a list of resin subheadings was exempt. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff**: +10% or +12.5% for most, 10% or 12.5% in total for the EU, Taiwan, Korea and Japan. China still pays its **2018–2019 Section 301 lists** (+25% on List 2 and 3 goods, +7.5% on List 4A), which USTR continued on October 7, 2026. Since **August 22, 2026** twenty Chapter 39 subheadings from Canada pay a **50% Section 338 duty**, even under USMCA. Antidumping and countervailing duty orders add company-specific duties on 12 plastics products; three of them — polypropylene corrugated boxes, acrylate monomers and oligomers, and fiberglass door panels — came under orders in 2026.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 39 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their exemptions (pharmaceutical-use resins, civil aircraft parts), the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 Lists 2, 3 and 4A and their product exclusions, the Canada Section 338 duty, Russia's rates in lieu of column 2, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. **Antidumping (AD) and countervailing (CVD) duty orders in force** on Chapter 39 goods (Federal Register, checked October 13, 2026): PET resin (3907.61) — AD on Canada, China, India and Oman, CVD on China and India; PET film, sheet and strip (3920.62) — AD on China, India, Taiwan and the UAE, CVD on India (continued March 27, 2026); polyethylene retail carrier bags (3923.21.00.85) — AD on China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, CVD on Vietnam; polyvinyl alcohol (3905.30) — AD on China and Japan (continued September 18, 2026); granular PTFE resin (3904.61.00.10) — AD and CVD on India and Russia; epoxy resins (3907.30) — AD on Korea, Taiwan and Thailand, CVD on Korea and Taiwan (May 27, 2025); multifunctional acrylate and methacrylate monomers and oligomers (3907.29, 3907.30, also Chapter 29 and 38 lines) — AD and CVD on Taiwan (March 11, 2026), AD on Korea (July 28, 2026); polypropylene corrugated boxes (3923.10.90) — AD and CVD on China (March 16, 2026), AD on Vietnam (July 17, 2026); fiberglass door panels (3925.20.00.10) — AD and CVD on China (August 6, 2026); laminated woven sacks (mainly 6305.33, also 3923.21, 3923.29, 3921.90 and 3917.39) — AD and CVD on China and Vietnam; plastic decorative ribbon (3920.20.00.15, 3926.40.00.10) — AD and CVD on China; and biaxial integral geogrids (3926.90.99) — AD and CVD on China. Under investigation: PTMEG (3907.29) from China, Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, and PFA fluoropolymer (3904.69.50) from India. AD/CVD rates are set per exporter and are not in the rate-by-country grid. Section 232: no Chapter 39 subheading is on the mandatory automobile-parts, truck-parts or metals lists. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: PET film orders continued
changes.detail: After sunset reviews, Commerce continued the antidumping orders on PET film, sheet and strip (3920.62) from China, India, Taiwan and the UAE and the countervailing duty order on India.

changes.title: Polypropylene corrugated boxes from China: AD and CVD orders
changes.detail: Antidumping (China-wide 83.64%) and countervailing (all-others 62.27%) duty orders on polypropylene corrugated boxes classified in 3923.10.90.00.

changes.title: Acrylate monomers and oligomers from Taiwan: AD and CVD orders
changes.detail: Antidumping (130.23%) and countervailing (103.43%) duty orders on multifunctional acrylate and methacrylate monomers and oligomers from Taiwan, entered under 3907.29, 3907.30 and Chapter 29 and 38 lines.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Eighteen Chapter 39 resin subheadings — among them 3901.90.90, 3902.90.00, 3904.61.00, 3907.10.00, 3907.21.00, 3911.90.25 and 3914.00.60 — were on the product exemption list (9903.03.03). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: India's extra 25% IEEPA duty removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) from February 7, 2026. The 25% reciprocal rate on India ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: PET sheet from Korea: antidumping order revoked
changes.detail: No domestic party took part in the first sunset review, so Commerce revoked the antidumping order on PET sheet (3920.62) from Korea, effective for entries from September 10, 2025.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: China Section 301 exclusions on nine Chapter 39 products extended to November 9, 2026
changes.detail: USTR extended 178 China Section 301 product exclusions through November 9, 2026, among them AA/AMPS terpolymers, polyethylene and coated films, other polyethylene bags (3923.21.00.95), PLA stopper-stirrers, sodium alginate resins, laboratory ware and sterile drapes (U.S. note 20(vvv), 9903.88.69). Matching goods skip the List 2, 3 or 4A duty; the 2026 Section 301 duty still applies.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84), on top of the 25% reciprocal rate in force since August 7, 2025 (EO 14326): 50% in all on Indian plastics, on top of the base rate. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: Thailand, Malaysia, Cambodia and Indonesia +19%, Vietnam +20%, India +25%, Korea +15%, the UK +10%. EU goods with a column 1 rate under 15% paid 15% in total — every Chapter 39 line. Resin subheadings on Annex II (9903.01.32) stayed exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Epoxy resins: AD orders on Korea, Taiwan and Thailand, CVD orders on Korea and Taiwan
changes.detail: Orders on epoxy resins (3907.30.00) — antidumping all-others rates 6.37% (Korea), 19.21% (Taiwan) and 5.25% (Thailand), countervailing all-others rates 1.30% (Korea) and 33.24% (Taiwan). The ITC found imports from China and India negligible, so no order was issued on them.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. Chinese polyethylene film then paid 4.2% + 25% (List 2) + 20% + 10% = 59.2% until November 9, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025, and paused the higher country rates announced on April 2 for other countries. With the 20% fentanyl duty and the 25% List 2 duty, Chinese polyethylene film (4.2% base) paid 174.2% until May 13, 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025, and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Chapter 39 resin subheadings on the Annex II exemption list (9903.01.32) — 18 in the list as last printed — were exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, on top of the Section 301 list duties. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China List 4A duty cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: Under the Phase One agreement USTR cut the List 4A duty (9903.88.15) from 15% to 7.5%. For Chapter 39 it covers 30 lines — plates and cups, sanitary ware, doors and windows, shutters and many 3926 articles.

changes.title: China List 4A reaches household plastics and builders' ware
changes.detail: The fourth China Section 301 list put +15% on Chinese plastic tableware, sanitary ware, builders' ware, alginates and other articles (9903.88.15).

changes.title: China List 3 duty raised to 25%
changes.detail: USTR raised the List 3 duty (9903.88.03) from 10% to 25%. For Chapter 39 List 3 covers 75 lines, among them plastic scrap, vinyl flooring, packaging, bags and bottles.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 reaches plastic packaging and flooring
changes.detail: The third China Section 301 list put +10% on Chinese plastic scrap, vinyl flooring, boxes, bags, bottles, closures and other articles.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 2 reaches plastic resins, film and sheet
changes.detail: The second China Section 301 list put +25% on Chinese polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PET and most other resins, plastic film and sheet, tape and foam (9903.88.02, 189 Chapter 39 lines).

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 39 goods were **$74.02B in 2025**, 5.4% less than the $78.23B of 2024 and well below the $89.88B peak of 2022. Articles of plastics made up 76% of it; the largest headings were **other plastic articles (3926)** at $14.61B, **packaging, bags and bottles (3923)** at $9.82B, **tableware and household articles (3924)** at $7.65B and **film and sheet (3920)** at $6.23B. Resins in primary forms (3901–3914) came to $17.71B, led by PET, polycarbonate and epoxy (3907, $4.26B) and polyethylene (3901, $3.77B).

**China** stayed the largest supplier at $16.87B but fell 21.6%; its trade is mostly finished articles — $5.84B of 3926 articles and $5.71B of household goods. **Canada** ($12.77B, -10.0%) is the main source of resins — $2.97B of polyethylene — and of film and packaging, and **Mexico** ($8.50B, +3.2%) of molded parts and packaging. **Vietnam** grew 30.1% to $4.78B, $2.19B of it vinyl flooring (3918), and **Thailand** grew 41.9% to $2.06B, with vinyl flooring its largest product too. Korea ($4.41B), Germany ($3.93B) and Japan ($2.83B) ship roughly half resins and half film, sheet and articles — Korea is the largest supplier of PET, polycarbonate and epoxy (3907) — while Taiwan ($2.70B) ships mainly packaging and articles.

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026 and the Canada Section 338 duties from August 22); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Chapter 39 base rates are low — Free to 6.5% — so the **extra duty by country** decides most of the cost. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026: **10% in total for Germany and the rest of the EU and for Taiwan**, **12.5% in total for Korea and Japan**, **+12.5% for Vietnam and Thailand**, **+10% for India and the UK**. **China adds 37.5%** on most resins, film, flooring and packaging (12.5% plus the 25% List 2 or List 3 duty), 20% on List 4A goods and 12.5% on the few lines on no list. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing; from Canada they pay nothing except on the **20 subheadings with the 50% Section 338 duty**, which no USMCA claim removes. Antidumping and countervailing duties on specific products and exporters come on top and are listed on the Tariff updates page.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 39: Plastics & Articles of Plastics — Import Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Plastics into the U.S.: TSCA Certification, FDA Food-Contact Rules, AD/CVD Scope & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 39) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 39 line needs at U.S. entry — TSCA certification for resins, FDA food-contact rules for packaging and tableware, CPSC rules for children's products, UFLPA tracing for PVC, AD/CVD deposits — and the legal ways to pay less: classification, origin, USMCA, the pharmaceutical-use and civil-aircraft exemptions, China exclusions, first sale, drawback and FTZ.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Plastics need few licenses, but three rules decide whether a shipment clears smoothly. **Resins and other polymers in bulk** (3901–3914) are chemical substances under TSCA: the importer must certify to CBP that they comply with TSCA, or that they are not subject to it. **Food-contact plastics** — bottles, closures, containers, tableware, packaging film — must be made only of substances FDA allows. And **PVC products from China** are a forced-labor high-priority sector, so CBP can hold them until the importer traces the supply chain back to the resin. Products covered by an **antidumping or countervailing duty order** also need a cash deposit at entry.

On cost, the base rate is small (Free to 6.5%) and the extra duty by country is large, so the levers that matter are the ones that change the country or the Chapter 99 treatment: the **country of origin** (+37.5% China, +12.5% Vietnam, 10% in total EU), **USMCA**, the **pharmaceutical-use** and **civil-aircraft** exemptions from the 2026 Section 301 duty, the **China product exclusions**, plus first-sale valuation, drawback and foreign-trade zones. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Classify correctly: primary form or article, polymer and form
levers.saves: The gap between line rates (Free to 6.5%) and, more often, between China lists: List 2 or 3 (+25%), List 4A (+7.5%) or no list
levers.appliesTo: All lines — for example resin (3901–3914) versus compound or article, film (3920) versus self-adhesive film (3919) or foam (3921), tableware (3924.10) versus packaging (3923)
levers.document: Technical data: polymer composition by weight, form (pellets, powder, liquid, sheet, article), cellular or not, adhesive or not, and use.
levers.caveat: Chapter note 4 classifies copolymers by the predominant comonomer, note 6 defines primary forms and note 10 limits 3920–3921 to flat products; a printed article may be Chapter 49 (section VII note 2). The declared line must match the goods; a ruling settles doubtful cases.

levers.title: Know the country of origin — and where a plastic article gets it
levers.saves: The difference between country rates: 10% in total for the EU or Taiwan, +12.5% for Vietnam, +37.5% for most Chinese plastics
levers.appliesTo: All lines; the gap is widest on Chinese film, flooring, packaging and bags
levers.document: Production records showing where the resin was polymerized and where the article was molded, extruded or converted.
levers.caveat: The Section 301 and 338 duties follow the country of origin: the country where the article was last substantially transformed. Repacking, cutting to length or printing may not change origin; CBP can ask for proof, and AD/CVD orders can reach goods finished in a third country.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 50–52

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 6.5%) plus the 10% Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: All lines from Mexico; from Canada, the lines not on the Section 338 list — all resins, polyethylene and PET film, pipe and most articles
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, kept ready for CBP.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on the 20 Canadian subheadings in U.S. note 51(b)(3). The good must meet the Chapter 39 rule of origin in General Note 11. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin)

levers.title: Claim the pharmaceutical-use exemption for resins
levers.saves: The 10%–12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.89) and the 25% Brazil duty (9903.05.06)
levers.appliesTo: The 32 resin subheadings in note 52(e) — 3901.90.90, 3902.90.00, PTFE 3904.61.00, vinyl polymers of 3905.91–3905.99, 3906.90.50, most of 3907 (including epoxy 3907.30 and PET 3907.61), nylon 3908, 3909.10, 3909.40, silicones 3910, 3911.20–3911.90, 3912.20–3912.90, 3913.90 and 3914.00 — when they are for use in pharmaceutical applications
levers.document: Evidence of the pharmaceutical end use (for example the buyer's use declaration and supply contract); report 9903.05.89 instead of the country heading.
levers.caveat: Only for goods actually used in pharmaceutical applications; it does not remove the China Section 301 list duties or AD/CVD.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 52(e), 50(a)(v)

levers.title: Claim the civil-aircraft exemptions
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.88), the Brazil duty (9903.05.05) and the Canada Section 338 duty (9903.03.16)
levers.appliesTo: Tubes, pipes and hoses of 3917.21–3917.40 and gaskets and other articles of 3926.90.45, 3926.90.94, 3926.90.96 and 3926.90.99 that are civil aircraft parts
levers.document: Proof that the goods meet general note 6 (certified for use in civil aircraft), and the matching Chapter 99 heading.
levers.caveat: Only for civil aircraft (not military or unmanned) articles that meet general note 6.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51(d), 52(d), 50(a)(iv)

levers.title: Use a China Section 301 product exclusion
levers.saves: The 25% List 2 or 3 duty, or the 7.5% List 4A duty, on matching Chinese goods
levers.appliesTo: 3906.90.50.00 (AA/AMPS terpolymers), 3913.10.00.00 (sodium alginate resins), 3919.10.20.55 and 3919.90.50.40/.60 (polyethylene film with acrylic adhesive), 3920.62.00.90 (PVdC- or PVOH-coated film), 3923.21.00.95 (other polyethylene bags), 3923.50.00.00 (PLA stopper-stirrers), 3926.90.99.15/.20 (laboratory ware), 3926.90.99.89 (sterile drapes and decanters)
levers.document: Product specifications showing the goods match the exclusion description; report 9903.88.69 instead of the list heading.
levers.caveat: In effect through November 9, 2026 unless USTR extends them. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.31) still applies.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20(vvv), 9903.88.69

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Every ad valorem duty is charged on a lower value — the base rate, the Section 301 and 338 duties and AD/CVD deposits included — when the factory price to a trading company is lower than the price you pay
levers.appliesTo: All lines bought through a trading company or agent rather than straight from the resin maker or molder
levers.document: Proof that the first sale was a bona fide sale for export to the United States at arm's length: the factory invoice, contracts and payment records.
levers.caveat: Only a sale clearly destined for the U.S. qualifies, and the importer must be able to show the earlier price at entry.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export or use to make exports
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported resin or film (or goods made from it) is exported or destroyed
levers.appliesTo: Any line — for example resin molded into parts that are exported, or packaging film used on exported goods
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import, manufacturing and export records.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check whether a given Chapter 99 duty or AD/CVD duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Process or hold goods in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: No duty on goods re-exported from the zone, and duty deferred until goods leave it for the U.S. market
levers.appliesTo: Any line — useful for resin compounders and converters that export part of their output
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's inventory records.
levers.caveat: Goods entered for U.S. consumption from a zone pay the duties in force on the entry date; TSCA and FDA rules still apply.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision for U.S. goods coming back
levers.saves: All duty on U.S.-made goods returned unchanged (9801.00.10), for example returned pallets of U.S. resin or rejected U.S. packaging
levers.appliesTo: Any line, for American goods returned without having been advanced in value or improved abroad
levers.document: Proof of U.S. origin and of the export, as CBP requires for the provision.
levers.caveat: The Section 301 and 338 duties also do not apply to goods properly entered under Chapter 98, except subchapter XXIII and 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 (U.S. notes 51(a) and 52(a)).

levers.title: Get a binding classification ruling
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate, the China list and AD/CVD scope: compound versus resin, film versus foam, a bag on or off the carrier-bag order, a Canadian article on or off the Section 338 list
levers.appliesTo: Any line where composition, form or use decides the line
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the article, its polymer content, form and use. AD/CVD scope questions go to Commerce.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a changed formulation may need a new one. CBP rulings do not decide AD/CVD scope.

rules.title: Resins and other polymers in bulk are TSCA chemical substances: before release the importer files a positive certification (they comply with TSCA) or a negative one (not subject to TSCA). Plastic articles need it only if a TSCA rule requires

Food-contact plastics (bottles, closures, containers, tableware, packaging) must be made only of substances FDA permits — for example olefin polymers meeting 21 CFR 177.1520. Food contact substances are outside FDA prior notice

Plastic products designed for children 12 or younger need third-party testing and a Children's Product Certificate, eFiled with the entry; child care articles (feeding and sleep items for children 3 or younger) may not contain the restricted phthalates
Plastic medical articles — surgical and exam gloves, face shields and masks, medical pads, sterile drapes — are medical devices: the foreign maker must register and list them with FDA

UFLPA: goods made wholly or in part in Xinjiang or by a company on the UFLPA Entity List are presumed made with forced labor and excluded. PVC is a high-priority sector: CBP asks for records tracing PVC products back to the ethylene and chlorine

citations.label: CBP forced labor operational guidance (PVC, Appendix A)

rules.title: Resin AD/CVD orders: PET resin (Canada, China, India, Oman; CVD China, India), polyvinyl alcohol (China, Japan), granular PTFE (India, Russia, AD and CVD), epoxy resins (Korea, Taiwan, Thailand; CVD Korea, Taiwan), acrylate monomers and oligomers (Taiwan AD and CVD, Korea AD). Cash deposits at entry; PTMEG and PFA are under investigation

Film and bag AD/CVD orders: PET film (China, India, Taiwan, UAE; CVD India), polyethylene retail carrier bags (China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam; CVD Vietnam), laminated woven sacks (China, Vietnam, AD and CVD), plastic decorative ribbon (China, AD and CVD)
Article AD/CVD orders: polypropylene corrugated boxes (China AD and CVD, Vietnam AD), fiberglass door panels (China, AD and CVD), biaxial integral geogrids (China, AD and CVD)
Country-of-origin marking in English, legible and permanent, on the article or, where the article cannot be marked, its container; bulk resin is marked on its bags or containers

Report the Chapter 99 headings with the line: the 2026 Section 301 heading for the country (or its exemption), the China list heading (9903.88.02, .03 or .15) or its exclusion (9903.88.69), Brazil (9903.05.01), Canada Section 338 (9903.03.14)

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 50–52

groups.label: Polyethylene & other ethylene polymers, in primary forms
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. Polyethylene is 6.5% (EVA 5.3%; elastomeric 3901.90.10 and the terpolymers of 3901.30.20 Free); Canada, the main supplier, is Free under USMCA and off the Section 338 list.

groups.label: Polypropylene & other olefin polymers, in primary forms
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. 6.5%; elastomeric polyisobutylene (3902.20.10) Free. Russian polypropylene pays 35% in place of column 2.

groups.label: Polystyrene, SAN & ABS, in primary forms
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. All 6.5%. No AD/CVD order.

groups.label: PVC, PTFE & other halogenated polymers, in primary forms
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. PVC is a UFLPA high-priority sector. Granular PTFE (3904.61.00.10) from India and Russia carries AD and CVD duties; PFA (3904.69.50) from India is under investigation.

groups.label: Polyvinyl acetate, polyvinyl alcohol & other vinyl polymers
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. Polyvinyl alcohol (3905.30) from China and Japan carries antidumping duties.

groups.label: Acrylic polymers, in primary forms
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. 3906.90.50 is on the pharmaceutical-use list and has a China exclusion for AA/AMPS terpolymers.

groups.label: PET, polycarbonates, epoxy resins, polyethers & other polyesters
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. AD/CVD on PET resin (3907.61), epoxy resins (3907.30) and acrylate oligomers (3907.29, 3907.30); PTMEG (3907.29) under investigation. Most subheadings are on the pharmaceutical-use list.

groups.label: Polyamides (nylon), in primary forms
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. Both nylon subheadings are on the pharmaceutical-use list.

groups.label: Amino resins, phenolic resins & polyurethanes
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. 3909.31 and 3909.39 (MDI-type polyurethanes) are on China List 3, the rest on List 2.

groups.label: Silicones, in primary forms
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. 3%; on the pharmaceutical-use list.

groups.label: Petroleum resins, polyterpenes & other resins
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. Free to 6.5%.

groups.label: Cellulose & its chemical derivatives
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. Cellulose acetates and ethers, 4.2%–6.4%.

groups.label: Natural polymers (alginates) & modified natural polymers
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. Sodium alginate resins from China are excluded from List 4A through November 9, 2026.

groups.label: Ion-exchange resins
groups.note: TSCA certification at entry. Free or 3.9%.

groups.label: Plastic waste, parings & scrap
groups.note: All Free. China List 3 adds 25%.

groups.label: Monofilament, rods, sticks & profile shapes
groups.note: PVC profiles fall under the UFLPA PVC sector. Russian 3916 goods pay column 2.

groups.label: Tubes, pipes, hoses & their fittings
groups.note: PVC pipe and hose fall under the UFLPA PVC sector. Civil-aircraft hoses and tubes (3917.21–3917.40) qualify for the Section 301, Brazil and Canada exemptions.

groups.label: Floor, wall & ceiling coverings, incl. vinyl flooring
groups.note: PVC flooring is named in CBP's PVC tracing guidance. Vinyl tile (3918.10.10) from Canada pays the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Self-adhesive tape, film, labels & other flat shapes
groups.note: Two polyethylene adhesive films from China are excluded from List 2 through November 9, 2026. 3919.10.20 and 3919.90.50 from Canada are on the Section 338 list.

groups.label: Film, sheet & strip, non-cellular and not reinforced
groups.note: Food-contact packaging film must meet FDA rules. PET film (3920.62) carries AD/CVD duties; polypropylene film (3920.20) from Canada is on the Section 338 list.

groups.label: Foam & other plastic sheet, film & strip
groups.note: Foam and other sheet; 3921.19 and 3921.90.50 from Canada are on the Section 338 list.

groups.label: Baths, sinks, toilet seats & other sanitary ware
groups.note: All 6.3%. Baths, sinks and toilet seats are on China List 4A (+7.5%), other sanitary ware on List 3.

groups.label: Packaging: boxes, bags, bottles, caps & closures
groups.note: Food-contact packaging must meet FDA rules. Carrier bags (3923.21.00.85) and PP corrugated boxes (3923.10.90) carry AD/CVD duties; most 3923 lines from Canada pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Tableware, kitchenware & household articles
groups.note: Food-contact tableware must meet FDA rules; children's items need CPSC certification. 3924.10.20, 3924.10.40 and 3924.90.56 from Canada are on the Section 338 list.

groups.label: Builders' ware: tanks, doors, windows, shutters
groups.note: Fiberglass door panels (3925.20.00.10) from China carry AD and CVD duties since August 6, 2026.

groups.label: Other articles: office supplies, gloves, fittings, gaskets
groups.note: Medical gloves, face shields and drapes are FDA devices. Civil-aircraft gaskets and articles (3926.90.45–.99) qualify for the aircraft exemptions; 3926.10, 3926.30, 3926.40 and 3926.90.99 from Canada are on the Section 338 list.

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 39: Plastics & Articles of Plastics — Tariff FAQ

seo.title: Plastic Tariffs FAQ 2026: China, Canada, Resin, PET, Bags & HS Codes for Plastics (HTS Ch. 39) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. tariffs on plastics: tariffs on plastic from China and Canada, plastic resin and PET tariffs, antidumping duties on PET resin and plastic bags, and the HS codes for plastic bags, plastic parts (3926.90), containers (3923), tableware (3924), film, PVC and polyethylene.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs and import rules for plastic resins, film, bags, packaging and other plastic products. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Base rates are low: 33 of the 319 Chapter 39 lines are Free and none is above 6.5% — most resins 6.5%, film 4.2%, bags and bottles 3%, plastic articles 5.3%.

Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty is added by country: +10% for India, the UK and non-USMCA goods from Canada and Mexico, +12.5% for Vietnam and Thailand, and a fixed total of 10% for the EU and Taiwan and 12.5% for Korea and Japan.
China pays the most: +12.5% plus +25% on its List 2 and 3 goods (resins, film, flooring, packaging, bags) — up to 44% — and +7.5% on List 4A goods; USTR continued the lists on October 7, 2026.

USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing. From Canada, 20 subheadings — plastic bags, bottles, closures, tableware, vinyl tile, PP film and others — pay a 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA; resins are not on the list.

Antidumping and countervailing duty orders cover 12 plastics products, among them PET resin, PET film, polyethylene carrier bags, epoxy, PVA, PTFE, polypropylene corrugated boxes and fiberglass door panels; PTMEG and PFA are under investigation.

The IEEPA duties ended February 24, 2026 and the 10% Section 122 surcharge on July 23, 2026. Resins need a TSCA certification at entry, food-contact plastics must meet FDA rules, and Chinese PVC goods face forced-labor tracing.

faqs.question: What is HTS Chapter 39?
faqs.answer: Chapter 39 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, "Plastics and Articles Thereof", covers plastics in primary forms (resins such as polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PET and epoxy, headings 3901–3914) and articles of plastics (scrap, pipes, flooring, tape, film and sheet, packaging, bags, tableware, builders' ware and other articles, headings 3915–3926). The 2026 Revision 21 has 319 tariff lines with base rates from Free to 6.5%.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on plastic imported into the U.S. in 2026?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every Chapter 39 line has a base rate of Free to 6.5%, and since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty is added for 60 economies: +10% for India, the UK and non-USMCA goods from Canada and Mexico, +12.5% for Vietnam and Thailand, 10% in total for the EU and Taiwan, 12.5% in total for Korea and Japan, and +12.5% plus up to +25% for China. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico pay nothing; 20 Canadian subheadings pay a 50% Section 338 duty. The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on plastic from China?
faqs.answer: Chinese plastics pay the base rate plus 12.5% (2026 Section 301, 9903.05.31) plus their 2018–2019 list duty: +25% on List 2 resins, film, sheet and tape and on List 3 scrap, flooring, packaging, bags and bottles, +7.5% on List 4A goods such as plates and cups. That is 44% on PVC or polyethylene resin, 41.7% on polyethylene film, 42.8% on vinyl flooring, 40.5% on plastic bags, 26.5% on plastic plates and 15.9% on food storage containers (on no list). AD/CVD duties add more on PET resin, PET film, carrier bags, PVA and other products. China supplied $16.87B in 2025, 21.6% less than in 2024.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on plastics from Canada?
faqs.answer: USMCA-qualifying plastics from Canada pay no base rate and no Section 301 duty, so Canadian polyethylene and other resins enter free. But 20 Chapter 39 subheadings — polyethylene bags, bottles, closures, boxes, tableware, vinyl tile, polypropylene film, foam sheet, tape, office supplies and other articles — pay a 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026, even under USMCA. Non-qualifying goods pay the base rate plus 10%, and 50% more on the listed lines. Canadian PET resin also carries an antidumping duty.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on plastic resin?
faqs.answer: Most resins (polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, polystyrene, PET) have a 6.5% base rate; PTFE is 5.8%, PVA 3.2%, silicones 3%. On top: +37.5% for China (List 2), 12.5% in total for Korea and Japan, 10% in total for EU and Taiwanese resin, +12.5% for Thailand, +10% for India, and nothing for USMCA-qualifying resin from Canada or Mexico. Resins used in pharmaceutical applications are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.89), and AD/CVD orders cover PET resin, PVA, PTFE, epoxy and acrylate oligomers from named countries.

faqs.question: Are there antidumping duties on PET resin and PET plastic?
faqs.answer: Yes. PET bottle resin (3907.61, 6.5%) from Canada, China, India and Oman is under antidumping orders, and from China and India under countervailing duty orders, continued in April 2022. PET film, sheet and strip (3920.62, 4.2%) from China, India, Taiwan and the UAE is under antidumping orders and Indian PET film under a countervailing duty order, continued March 27, 2026. The PET sheet order on Korea was revoked from September 10, 2025. Cash-deposit rates are set per exporter and come on top of the base rate and Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for plastic bags?
faqs.answer: Sacks and bags of polyethylene are 3923.21 and of other plastics 3923.29, both 3%; polyethylene retail carrier bags with handles are 3923.21.00.85. Retail carrier bags from China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam carry antidumping duties (Vietnam also countervailing). Chinese bags pay 40.5% (3% + 12.5% + 25% List 3) before AD duty, Vietnamese 15.5%, and Canadian bags 50% even under USMCA.

faqs.question: What is HS code 3926.90 and what is the tariff on plastic parts?
searchedAs: hts code for plastic molded parts
faqs.answer: 3926.90 covers other articles of plastics not specified elsewhere in Chapter 39 — molded parts, clips, cable ties, gaskets, laboratory ware, face shields; most fall in 3926.90.99 at 5.3%. Parts of machines, vehicles or instruments are classified with those goods (chapter note 2), not here. A 3926.90.99 article pays 15.3% from India or the UK, 17.8% from Vietnam, 10% from the EU, 25.3% from China (List 4A) and 50% from Canada even under USMCA (Section 338). It was the largest Chapter 39 import, $11.23B in 2025.

faqs.question: What is HS code 3923?
faqs.answer: Heading 3923 covers articles for the conveyance or packing of goods: boxes, cases and crates (3923.10, 3%), sacks and bags (3923.21, 3923.29, 3%), bottles and similar containers (3923.30, 3%), spools (3923.40, 5.3%), caps, lids and closures (3923.50, 5.3%) and other packaging (3923.90, 3%). Polypropylene corrugated boxes (3923.10.90) from China and Vietnam and carrier bags carry AD/CVD duties. Food-contact packaging must meet FDA rules.

faqs.question: What is HS code 3924 for plastic tableware and household articles?
faqs.answer: 3924.10 is plastic tableware and kitchenware — plates, cups and bowls 6.5% (3924.10.20), trays 5.3%, dispensers and other items 3.4% (3924.10.40) — and 3924.90 other household and toilet articles such as shower curtains, hangers and bathroom articles (3.1%–3.4%). From China plates and cups pay 26.5% (List 4A) and other kitchenware 15.9%. Food-contact items must meet FDA rules; children's items need a CPSC certificate.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for plastic film and sheet?
faqs.answer: Non-cellular, unreinforced film and sheet are heading 3920: polyethylene film 3920.10 (4.2%), polypropylene 3920.20 (4.2%), PVC 3920.43–3920.49 (3.1%–5.8%), acrylic sheet 3920.51, polycarbonate 3920.61 (5.8%) and PET 3920.62 (4.2%). Self-adhesive film and tape are 3919, and foam or reinforced sheet 3921. Chinese film and sheet pay 37.5%–44% (List 2); PET film from China, India, Taiwan and the UAE also carries AD duties.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for PVC?
faqs.answer: PVC resin not mixed with other substances is 3904.10 (6.5%), plasticized or mixed PVC 3904.21–3904.22. Rigid PVC pipe is 3917.23 (3.1%), PVC profiles 3916.20 (5.8%), PVC flooring 3918.10 (4.2%–6.5%; vinyl tile 3918.10.10, 5.3%) and PVC film and sheet 3920.43–3920.49. PVC is a UFLPA high-priority sector, so CBP can ask importers of Chinese PVC goods to trace the supply chain to the resin.

faqs.question: What is the tariff code for polyethylene?
faqs.answer: Polyethylene in primary forms is heading 3901: specific gravity under 0.94 (LDPE, LLDPE) 3901.10, 0.94 or more (HDPE) 3901.20, EVA 3901.30 and ethylene-alpha-olefin copolymers 3901.40 — mostly 6.5%. Canada supplied $2.97B of the $3.77B imported in 2025, Free under USMCA. Chinese polyethylene pays 44% (List 2 or 3), Korean 12.5% and EU 10% in total. A TSCA certification is required at entry.
